text: {"answer":"The evidence largely says no, raising the minimum wage does not substantially reduce overall employment, though the picture is contested. A meta-regression of 16 UK studies finds no overall practically significant adverse employment effect, with a possible genuine adverse effect in residential home care [5f591435f1d8#0]. A review co-authored by Dube reports that most US minimum wage studies find no job losses or only small disemployment effects [f3df8a818b8c#0], and a study of low-wage jobs finds the overall number essentially unchanged over five years, with some reduction in tradeable sectors [e0f83db9d354#1]. Nursing facility studies find no reduction in hours worked by lower-paid nurses [fb83e4fd4a0d#1]. The contradicting side is real: Congressional Budget Office estimates for a $15 federal minimum project about 1.4 million fewer jobs [6de9116294ca#3], and older work on youth employment reports declines of roughly 1 to 2 percent per 10 percent increase [ad8b67a3ca55#10]. Overall, the weight of recent evidence favours small or no employment effects, but effects vary by group, sector and wage level, so confidence is moderate.","confidence":68,"one_line":"Mostly no: recent reviews find little or no overall job loss, but teen and some sector effects and CBO projections show measurable reductions."}
